title: Variables & Data Types
summary: A variable is a named place for a value. Its type tells Java which values and operations are allowed.

sections.title: Your first Java program
sections.text: The JDK contains the compiler and development tools. javac turns Main.java into bytecode; the JVM runs that bytecode. In this workspace use public class Main and public static void main(String[] args). Statements end with semicolons; braces group code; // begins a comment.

sections.title: Choose a type
sections.text: Java has eight primitive types: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, and boolean. Start with int for whole numbers, long for large counts, double for approximations, char for one UTF-16 code unit, and boolean for true/false. String is a reference type. Use 5L for a long literal and single quotes for a char.

sections.title: Assignment and conversion
sections.text: int age = 19 declares and initializes a variable. age = 20 changes it; final int LIMIT = 100 cannot be reassigned. Local variables must be initialized before use. Widening int to long is automatic. Narrowing double to int needs a cast and discards the fractional part. Integer overflow wraps rather than raising an exception.

walkthrough: println prints 14 followed by a newline.
pitfall: long result = a * b still multiplies two ints first. Use (long) a * b when the product may overflow int.
complexity: A fixed number of primitive assignments and arithmetic operations takes O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

title: Input / Output
summary: Programs receive input, process it, and produce output in an agreed format.

sections.title: Read tokens and lines
sections.text: Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in) creates an input reader. nextInt(), nextLong(), and nextDouble() read typed tokens; next() reads one word. nextLine() reads the remainder of the current line, including spaces. Check hasNextInt() when malformed input is possible.

sections.title: Print precisely
sections.text: System.out.print leaves the cursor on the same line; println adds a newline. printf uses placeholders such as %d and %.2f; %n is a platform newline. Automated judges expect exactly the required answer: avoid prompts such as Enter a number. Whitespace still matters inside a line.

sections.title: Faster input and output
sections.text: For larger datasets, BufferedReader plus StringTokenizer reads lines and tokens efficiently; methods may throw IOException. Accumulate many output values in StringBuilder. title: Operators
summary: Operators calculate values, compare them, and combine conditions. Evaluation order is part of the logic.

sections.title: Arithmetic and precedence
sections.text: Use +, -, *, /, and %. With integer operands, division truncates toward zero. % gives the remainder; its sign follows the dividend. Multiplication and division bind more tightly than addition. Parentheses make intent clear. A zero integer divisor throws ArithmeticException.

sections.title: Comparison and logic
sections.text: <, <=, >, >=, ==, and != produce booleans. && and || short-circuit: the right side is evaluated only if needed. ! negates a boolean. Use equals for String content. A condition such as x >= 0 && x < n expresses two checks; Java does not allow 0 <= x < n.

sections.title: Updates and bits
sections.text: += updates a value. Prefix ++x increments before yielding a value; postfix x++ yields the old value. Avoid multiple updates inside a single expression. &, |, ^, ~, <<, >>, and >>> operate on bits; && and || are the usual boolean choices. The ternary condition ? a : b chooses one expression.

walkthrough: Both comparisons are true, so the conjunction is true.
pitfall: == compares String references, not content. Also, double value = 5/2 stores 2.0 because integer division happens first.
complexity: A fixed number of primitive arithmetic and boolean operations is O(1) time and O(1) space.

title: if-else & switch
summary: Conditional control flow chooses which instructions run. Put the most specific conditions in the right order.

sections.title: Branches
sections.text: An if block runs only when its condition is true. else if checks another condition only if earlier ones were false; else covers the remaining cases. Independent if statements may all run. Always use braces while learning to avoid misleading indentation.

sections.title: Multiway selection
sections.text: Traditional switch matches discrete case labels; without break, execution can fall through into later cases. A default handles unmatched values. title: Loops
summary: A loop repeats work while changing some state. A correct loop has a clear start, condition, and update.

sections.title: for and while
sections.text: Use for when initialization, test, and update belong together: for(int i=0;i<n;i++). Use while when repetition depends on a changing condition. Conditions are checked before the body. A do-while checks afterward, so its body runs at least once.

sections.title: Accumulators and control
sections.text: A running sum begins at 0; a running product usually begins at 1. Update the accumulator once per value. break exits the nearest loop; continue skips the rest of the current iteration. Ensure the update still happens when continue is used in a while loop.

sections.title: Nested loops and invariants
sections.text: A loop invariant is something true before every iteration, such as sum equals all values processed so far. For a nested n-by-m traversal, the inner loop runs m times for each outer iteration: n*m operations. A loop index is not always the same as the value you process.

walkthrough: i becomes 5; the condition fails; 10 is printed.
pitfall: i<=array.length accesses one index too many. Array loops normally use i<array.length. A missing update can create an infinite loop.
complexity: Summing 1..n using a loop takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

title: Dry Run / Tracing
summary: A dry run simulates a program on paper before executing it. Record state changes instead of guessing the final answer.

sections.title: Build a trace table
sections.text: Use columns for the current statement or iteration, relevant variables, conditions, and output so far. Record values after each assignment. A variable may change many times in a single loop, so a single final row is not enough to explain the behavior.

sections.title: Track decisions explicitly
sections.text: Write true or false for each condition. For short-circuit operators, mark skipped expressions. For array operations, show indexes and stored values separately. When a method returns, record the returned value at its call site.

sections.title: Use traces to debug
sections.text: Start with a tiny normal input, then an edge case. Compare the first differing state with your intended invariant. Compiler errors mean the program could not start; runtime errors happen during execution; logic errors can finish normally with wrong output.

walkthrough: i=2: total=12, x=8; the next condition fails.
pitfall: Do not use an updated value too early. In total+=x; x+=2;, the addition uses x before the increment.
complexity: A trace of k executed statements costs O(k) time; storing every row costs O(k) space.

sections.title: Extract decimal digits
sections.text: For a non-negative integer n, n%10 is its last digit and n/10 removes that digit. Repeating these operations processes digits from right to left. Zero has one decimal digit, so a do-while or explicit zero case is needed for counting digits.

sections.title: Rebuild and compare
sections.text: To reverse digits, update reversed = reversed*10 + digit. Keep a copy of the original when checking a palindrome. Trailing zeros disappear when represented as an integer: reversing 120 gives 21. Use long and define an overflow policy.

sections.title: Factors and primes
sections.text: A prime is greater than 1 and has no divisors other than 1 and itself. If n has a factor larger than its square root, its paired factor is smaller. Check divisors through sqrt(n); i<=n/i avoids i*i overflow for positive n.

pitfall: A while(n>0) loop runs zero times for n=0. That is fine for digit sum, but digit count must return 1.
complexity: Digit extraction takes O(d) time for d decimal digits and O(1) auxiliary space.

sections.title: Rows before symbols

title: Methods

sections.title: Signatures and return values

Checked exceptions such as IOException must be caught or declared; unchecked exceptions such as IllegalArgumentException usually indicate a violated contract. title: OOP Basics
summary: Object-oriented programming groups related state and behavior, while controlling how that state can change.

sections.title: Classes and objects
sections.text: A class defines fields and methods; new creates an instance. A constructor initializes that instance and has no return type. this refers to the current object. sections.title: Encapsulation and abstraction
sections.text: Encapsulation protects representation details behind an API. An interface describes a contract; an implementing class supplies behavior. sections.title: Inheritance and polymorphism
sections.text: A subclass extends one class and may implement multiple interfaces. Overriding supplies a subclass implementation with a compatible signature; dynamic dispatch selects it at runtime. Overloading chooses among parameter lists at compile time. equals defines logical equality; equal objects must share a hashCode.

sections.title: Essential Java bridge
sections.text: Packages organize classes; imports shorten type names. public, protected, package-private, and private control access. Generics such as List<Integer> provide compile-time type checks; collections use wrapper types, not int. Autoboxing converts int to Integer; unboxing null throws NullPointerException. title: Time & Space Complexity

sections.text: O(1) is constant; O(log n) grows by repeated halving; O(n) scans; O(n log n) is common for efficient comparison sorts; O(n²) often checks all pairs. sections.title: Space and recursion

title: Queue — Java collection
summary: Queue models first-in, first-out processing: arrivals are handled in their arrival order.

sections.title: FIFO operations

sections.title: Choose the implementation
sections.text: ArrayDeque is a common efficient FIFO queue. LinkedList also implements Queue. PriorityQueue implements Queue too, but removes by priority rather than arrival time, so the interface name alone does not guarantee FIFO.

sections.title: Breadth-first work

title: PriorityQueue
summary: PriorityQueue exposes the highest-priority element; by default in Java, the smallest element has priority.

sections.title: Heap behavior
sections.text: PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(); offer inserts, peek returns the smallest, and poll removes it. The heap maintains a partial order, not a fully sorted array. Repeated polling yields priority order; iteration does not.

sections.title: Custom order
sections.text: Use Comparator.reverseOrder() for a max-priority queue. For objects, compare the relevant field using Integer.compare or Comparator.comparingInt, then define tie-breakers if deterministic order matters. Do not mutate priority fields while an object is inside the queue.

sections.title: Top-k pattern
sections.text: To keep the k largest values, maintain a min-heap of size at most k. Insert each value and remove the minimum when size exceeds k. The smallest retained element is the current kth-largest. Validate k against input length.

pitfall: Printing or iterating the queue does not guarantee sorted order. Poll repeatedly to observe priority order.
complexity: offer/poll are O(log n); peek is O(1); space is O(n).

title: Comparator
summary: A comparator defines a consistent ordering between two objects. It is central to sorting and priority queues.

sections.title: The comparison contract
sections.text: compare(a,b) returns a negative number if a comes before b, zero for a tie, and a positive number after. Only the sign matters. Ordering must be transitive and sign-symmetric; inconsistent comparisons can break sorting or ordered collections.

sections.title: Safe comparisons
sections.text: Use Integer.compare(a,b) or Long.compare(a,b), not subtraction that can overflow. Comparator.comparingInt(Item::score) orders by a field. A lambda such as (a,b)->Integer.compare(a.score,b.score) implements the interface; understand classes and methods first.

sections.title: Tie-breakers and reversal
sections.text: thenComparing adds a tie-breaker. reversed reverses the comparator built so far, so its placement matters. For nullable values, use nullsFirst or nullsLast deliberately. TreeSet treats compare==0 as duplicate ordering keys, which may differ from equals.

pitfall: return a-b can overflow and reverse the sign. Use comparison methods instead.
complexity: Sorting n items with constant-time comparisons is O(n log n) time; comparisons on long strings can cost more.

sections.title: Collections versus Arrays

title: Sorting
summary: Sorting arranges values by an order and makes many later algorithms easier.

sections.title: Elementary sorts
sections.text: Selection sort repeatedly finds the next minimum; insertion sort shifts larger preceding values; bubble sort swaps out-of-order neighbors. Their usual worst-case time is O(n²). Insertion sort can be O(n) on already sorted input and works well for small or nearly sorted data.

sections.title: Divide-and-conquer sorts
sections.text: Merge sort sorts halves and merges in O(n log n) time, usually using O(n) auxiliary storage for arrays. Quicksort partitions around a pivot; typical randomized performance is O(n log n), but worst-case time can be O(n²). Do not promise worst-case O(n log n) for naive quicksort.

sections.title: Stability and mutation
sections.text: A stable sort keeps equal-key records in original relative order. In-place algorithms use small extra storage, though recursion also counts. Java object sorting is stable; primitive sorting has no object identity stability to preserve. Test negatives, duplicates, and already sorted arrays.

walkthrough: The sorted prefix grows by one at each outer iteration.
pitfall: Using >= instead of > in insertion sort shifts equal items too and can destroy stability.
complexity: Insertion sort uses O(n²) worst-case time, O(n) best-case time, and O(1) auxiliary space.

title: Binary Search
summary: Binary search discards half a search interval at each step, using a sorted order or a monotone predicate.

sections.title: Sorted-array search
sections.text: Maintain inclusive bounds lo and hi. Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)/2. If a[mid] is too small, use lo=mid+1; if too large, use hi=mid-1. Equality returns a match. An empty interval means absence. Keep one boundary convention throughout.

sections.title: Bounds and duplicates
sections.text: Lower bound finds the first index with value>=target, or n if none. A half-open [lo,hi) interval with hi=n is convenient: if a[mid]>=target, hi=mid; otherwise lo=mid+1. This handles duplicates and avoids returning an arbitrary equal element.

sections.title: Search on an answer
sections.text: A feasibility predicate must change in only one direction, such as impossible then possible as capacity rises. Prove monotonicity and choose bounds containing an answer. Each predicate evaluation can cost more than O(1), so multiply its cost by the number of search iterations.

walkthrough: [0,1): mid=0, value=1, move lo to 1; stop.
pitfall: Using lo=mid in the wrong interval convention can stop the interval from shrinking and cause an infinite loop.
complexity: Array binary search takes O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space iteratively.

sections.title: Find repeated work
sections.text: Look for rescanning, recomputing the same sum, repeated membership tests, or overlapping subproblems. Prefix sums, maps, sorting, two pointers, and memoization remove different kinds of repetition. Choose based on the structure rather than the name of a pattern.

sections.title: Preserve correctness

sections.title: Node structure

sections.title: Traversal and cycles

sections.title: Search, insert, delete
sections.text: Search or insert follows one child based on comparison. Delete a leaf directly; replace a one-child node by its child. For two children, replace with the inorder successor and delete that successor in the right subtree. Reassign the returned subtree root.

sections.title: Height determines cost
sections.text: Operations take O(h), which is O(log n) in a balanced tree but O(n) in a skewed one. Inorder produces sorted keys. Java TreeMap/TreeSet use balanced search trees; a handwritten naive BST does not balance itself.

title: Heap
summary: A binary heap keeps the best-priority element at the root while storing a complete binary tree in an array.

sections.title: Array relationships
sections.text: For zero-based index i, children are 2*i+1 and 2*i+2; the parent is (i-1)/2 for i>0. A min-heap has each parent no greater than its children. Siblings need not be ordered. Completeness keeps height logarithmic.

sections.title: Sift operations
sections.text: Insert at the end and sift up while it violates the parent relation. To remove the minimum, move the last value to the root, reduce size, and sift down by exchanging with the smaller child. Always check child bounds.

sections.title: Build and sort
sections.text: Bottom-up heap construction sifts down internal nodes and takes O(n), not O(n log n). Repeated insertion takes O(n log n). Heapsort repeatedly moves the root to the sorted end; it is O(n log n), in-place for an array, and not stable in its usual form.

walkthrough: Each child is compared with its parent.

title: Recursion
summary: Advanced recursion requires defining exactly what each call means and how its smaller results combine.

sections.title: Recurrence and work
sections.text: A recurrence models work, such as T(n)=T(n-1)+O(1) for linear recursion or T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) for merge sort. Count repeated subproblems separately from maximum call depth. Two recursive branches can create exponential work while depth remains linear.

sections.title: Divide and conquer
sections.text: Split a problem into smaller independent parts, solve them, then combine. Balanced splitting gives logarithmic depth, but the combine step determines total work. Avoid copying large subarrays unnecessarily; pass index ranges where possible.

sections.title: Memoization and safety
sections.text: When the same pure subproblem repeats, cache its result using a complete state key. A missing state dimension causes incorrect reuse. Validate base cases and bounds. For very deep traversals, replace recursion with an explicit stack.

walkthrough: Each result reuses the saved half power twice.
pitfall: Calling power(a,b/2) twice duplicates the work. Save the returned result and reuse it.
complexity: Fast power uses O(log b) time and O(log b) recursive space, assuming bounded-cost arithmetic.

title: Backtracking

sections.title: Choose, explore, undo
sections.text: A call represents a partial solution. Choose a next option, modify the state, recurse, and undo the modification. When the solution is complete, save a copy. Keeping the same mutable list reference corrupts previously saved answers.

sections.title: Prune carefully

title: Greedy
summary: A greedy algorithm commits to a locally best choice. Its correctness needs a proof that the choice can belong to an optimum.

sections.title: Choice and proof
sections.text: An exchange argument shows how to replace part of an optimal solution with the greedy choice without making it worse. A local rule that looks sensible is not enough. Search for small counterexamples before trusting it.

sections.title: Intervals and ordering
sections.text: To maximize the number of non-overlapping intervals, sort by finish time and repeatedly take a compatible interval. Define endpoint compatibility: here [start,end) allows the next interval to start exactly when the previous ends. Earliest start or shortest length is not generally the right rule.

sections.title: Know the limits
sections.text: Taking the largest coin first fails for arbitrary denominations: with 1,3,4, target 6 is best as 3+3, not 4+1+1. Some problems need DP or backtracking. Greedy solutions often combine sorting or heaps with one pass.

walkthrough: Take the first two, reject the overlapping [2,5).
pitfall: Greedy coin change is not correct for every denomination set. Validate the proof rather than memorizing a rule.
complexity: Interval scheduling sorts in O(n log n) then scans in O(n); auxiliary storage depends on the sort.

title: Graphs
summary: A graph models entities and relationships. Decide direction, weights, and connectivity before choosing an algorithm.

sections.title: Represent the graph
sections.text: An adjacency list stores neighbors for each vertex using O(V+E) space. An undirected edge is added in both directions; a directed edge only one. An adjacency matrix takes O(V²) space but gives constant-time edge lookup. Label vertices 0..V-1 and handle isolated vertices.

sections.title: BFS and DFS
sections.text: BFS uses a queue and finds shortest path lengths in an unweighted graph. DFS explores deeply using recursion or a stack. Mark visited when discovering a vertex. To traverse disconnected graphs, start again from every still-unvisited vertex.

sections.title: Next algorithms
sections.text: Topological sorting applies to directed acyclic graphs. Dijkstra requires non-negative edge weights; use long distances and ignore stale heap entries. Union Find maintains disjoint components with path compression and union by size/rank. MST algorithms solve a different goal from shortest paths.

title: Dynamic Programming
summary: Dynamic programming reuses solutions to overlapping subproblems. Begin with a precise state, not with a table.

sections.title: State, transition, base
sections.text: State exactly what dp[i] or dp[i][j] means. A transition derives a state from smaller solved states. Base cases represent the smallest valid inputs; impossible states need a deliberate sentinel. For climbing stairs, ways[0]=1 and ways[n]=ways[n-1]+ways[n-2].

sections.title: Memoization and tabulation
sections.text: Memoization starts with recursion and caches visited states. Tabulation fills states in dependency order. Time is roughly number of states times work per transition. Space optimization is valid only when discarded states are no longer needed.

sections.title: Major families
sections.text: Learn one-dimensional choices, grid paths, 0/1 knapsack, subset sum, LIS, and string DP. In 0/1 knapsack, a one-dimensional capacity loop runs backward so one item is not reused; unbounded variants often run forward. Explain why a greedy rule is insufficient before reaching for DP.

complexity: Climbing stairs takes O(n) time and O(n) table space; keeping only the previous two states reduces space to O(1).
